Lateral epicondyle tenderness.text: Point tenderness directly over the extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) origin at the lateral epicondyle localizes the lesion to the common extensor origin — the hallmark finding produced by repetitive eccentric wrist-extension overload causing angiofibroblastic tendinosis of the ECRB.
Lateral epicondyle tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.6; Nirschl & Ashman, angiofibroblastic tendinosis model

No swelling.text: Absence of swelling supports a chronic degenerative tendinosis rather than an acute inflammatory, bursal, or joint process, consistent with the overuse pathophysiology underlying lateral epicondylalgia.

Poor scapular support.text: Weak scapular stabilizers force the distal wrist extensors to work harder to control the hand during upper-limb tasks, increasing cumulative eccentric load on the ECRB and perpetuating the tendinopathy — a proximal-to-distal loading fault recognized in lateral epicondylalgia rehabilitation.

Wrist-loading grip.text: A grip pattern that keeps the wrist extensors under sustained tension during gripping reproduces the repetitive eccentric loading mechanism that drives ECRB microtrauma — the same biomechanical stress isolated by Cozen's and Mill's testing.

findings: Resisted wrist extension strong but painful at the lateral epicondyle — this app's own library flags this as the "most important elbow test"
Cozen's and Mill's tests reproduce the same finding in different arm positions
sttt.interpretation: Resisted Wrist Extension is documented as the most important elbow test in this library; Cozen's and Mill's are this same resisted test performed in different arm positions, both reproducing pain at the lateral epicondyle.

cpa.pattern: Inhibited wrist extensors (ECRB/ECRL) with compensatory overactive wrist flexors — the literal documented interpretation for lateral epicondylalgia in this app's library. Fascial component (from source): Deep-back-arm line / common extensor fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Lateral Epicondyle Load Test (Cozen's / Mill's / Maudsley's)
functionalScreen.note: The named functional screen for exactly this condition. FMA source note: Resisted wrist extension (Cozen's/Mill's) & gripping reproduce pain.

Medial epicondyle tenderness.text: Point tenderness at the common flexor-pronator origin (FCR/FCU/pronator teres) localizes the lesion to the medial epicondyle — the mirror-image tendinopathy to lateral epicondylalgia, but affecting the wrist flexor/pronator mass rather than the extensors.

Wrist-flexor-loading grip posture.text: Repetitive gripping with the wrist held in flexion and pronation (e.g. golf swing, throwing, manual labour) places sustained eccentric load on the flexor-pronator origin — the same mechanism reproduced by the Golfer's elbow test.

findings: Resisted wrist flexion strong but painful at the medial epicondyle
The Golfer's elbow test IS this same resisted test plus pronation
sttt.interpretation: The Golfer's elbow test is the resisted wrist-flexion test performed with added pronation; a strong-but-painful response at the medial epicondyle confirms a contractile pattern.

cpa.pattern: Overactive wrist flexors (FCR/FCU) — check wrist extensor inhibition as the driver of this pattern. Fascial component (from source): Common flexor–pronator fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Medial Elbow / Valgus Screen
functionalScreen.note: This screen directly names "Golfer's Elbow" as one of its target conditions. FMA source note: Resisted wrist flexion/pronation reproduce medial pain.

Antecubital tenderness ± gap/retraction.text: Tenderness over the antecubital fossa without a palpable gap suggests early tendinopathy, whereas a palpable defect with proximal muscle-belly retraction (Popeye deformity) indicates complete tendon rupture from its radial tuberosity insertion, the retraction reflecting the unopposed pull of the biceps once its distal anchor is lost.
Antecubital tenderness ± gap/retraction.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.6; O'Driscoll et al., Hook Test for distal biceps rupture

Anterior-arm loading.text: Postures or activities that load the elbow into resisted flexion-supination (e.g. heavy eccentric lifting) reproduce the mechanism of distal biceps tendon overload and failure, historically associated with a single forceful eccentric contraction against resistance.

resisted.label: Resisted Elbow Flexion (supinated)
options: Weak + Painless with palpable gap/Popeye deformity (rupture)

findings: Resisted elbow flexion (supinated) strong but painful at the antecubital fossa suggests tendinopathy
Weak & painless with a palpable gap/Popeye deformity suggests complete rupture — confirmed by the hook test
sttt.interpretation: A strong-but-painful resisted elbow flexion (supinated) at the antecubital fossa points to tendinopathy; if instead weak and painless with a palpable gap and Popeye deformity, the hook test confirms a complete distal biceps rupture.

muscles.name: Biceps Brachii
muscles.state: Overactive proximally (RC compensation) if tendinopathy — structural, not compensation-driven, if ruptured

cpa.pattern: If overactive proximally (rotator-cuff compensation) it can predispose to distal overload and tendinopathy; if ruptured, this is a structural injury, not a compensation pattern. Fascial component (from source): Deep-front arm line (biceps).

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Elbow AROM (supination component)
functionalScreen.note: General baseline only — no dedicated distal-biceps FMA test exists in this app's library; the resisted/hook test above remains primary.

Reduced extension.text: Terminal extension loss is the earliest and most consistent ROM finding in elbow OA, reflecting osteophyte formation at the olecranon/coronoid fossae and anterior capsular fibrosis — consistent with the elbow's capsular pattern of flexion restricted more than extension.
Reduced extension.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.6 (capsular pattern of the elbow)

crepitus.text: Palpable or audible crepitus during motion reflects roughened, degenerated articular cartilage and osteophytic irregularity grinding across the joint surfaces — a direct mechanical sign of the degenerative process.

± loose-body locking.text: Intermittent mechanical locking or catching indicates a loose osteochondral or osteophytic fragment intermittently interposing within the joint, producing a springy rather than hard end-feel and true locking episodes distinct from simple capsular stiffness.

Fixed-flexion posture.text: A resting elbow flexion contracture develops as the anterior capsule fibroses and shortens in response to chronic effusion and osteophyte formation — the joint settles into the position of maximum capsular volume/comfort, characteristic of degenerative and post-traumatic elbow OA.

findings: Resisted tests generally painless — non-contractile pattern
Passive flexion/extension both restricted in a capsular pattern (flexion limited more than extension)
End-feel hard/bony, or springy if loose bodies are present
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing rules out a contractile source; a capsular-pattern restriction (flexion more limited than extension) with a hard/bony end-feel is consistent with osteoarthritis, while a springy end-feel instead suggests loose bodies.

cpa.reason: Not primarily compensation-driven (joint OA); Triceps/Biceps facilitation supports function around the restricted arc. Fascial component (from source): Anterior capsule fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Elbow AROM (flexion/extension/pronation/supination)
functionalScreen.note: The direct match for a capsular-pattern assessment of this condition.

Posterior fluctuant swelling over olecra.text: A discrete, fluctuant, superficial swelling directly over the olecranon reflects fluid distension of the subcutaneous olecranon bursa — an inert, non-articular structure — distinguishing this from a true joint effusion or intra-articular process.

Elbow-resting-on-surface loading.text: Repetitive or sustained direct pressure on the posterior elbow (e.g. leaning on a desk or hard surface) is the classic mechanical trigger for olecranon bursal irritation and fluid accumulation.

Olecranon.text: Direct palpation over the olecranon localizes the swelling to the bursa itself rather than the joint line, confirming a superficial rather than intra-articular source.

Fluctuance/temperature assessment.text: Fluctuance confirms a fluid-filled bursal sac; increased local warmth or erythema raises suspicion for septic bursitis and should prompt referral for aspiration and culture rather than routine conservative management.
Fluctuance/temperature assessment.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.6; septic bursitis differential

resisted.label: Resisted Elbow Extension
options: Painful (direct posterior pressure loading the bursa)

findings: Resisted elbow extension usually painless — the bursa is an inert, non-contractile structure
Painful only if direct posterior pressure loads the bursa
Palpation/fluctuance is the primary test for this condition
sttt.interpretation: The bursa is inert, not contractile, so resisted elbow extension is usually painless unless direct posterior pressure loads it; palpation and fluctuance assessment remain the primary tests.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (bursal inflammation, often trauma/pressure-related). Fascial component (from source): Posterior olecranon fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.reason: Not directly covered — palpation/fluctuance (STTT, above) remains the primary tool; Elbow AROM only as a general baseline.

Medial tenderness.text: Tenderness along the anterior bundle of the UCL, from the medial epicondyle to the sublime tubercle, localizes the lesion to the primary medial elbow stabilizer against valgus stress, most commonly injured in overhead throwing athletes.

valgus laxity (thrower).text: Palpable increased medial joint-line gapping under valgus stress in a throwing athlete indicates compromise of the anterior bundle UCL's restraint function — the structure loaded most heavily during the late-cocking and early-acceleration phases of throwing.
valgus laxity (thrower).source: O'Driscoll, Lawton & Smith, Moving Valgus Stress Test (Am J Sports Med, 2005)

Valgus-loading throwing posture.text: The late-cocking through early-acceleration phase of the throwing motion generates the highest valgus torque at the elbow, directly loading the anterior bundle of the UCL — the repetitive-overload mechanism underlying UCL sprain in throwers.
Valgus-loading throwing posture.source: O'Driscoll, Lawton & Smith, Moving Valgus Stress Test (Am J Sports Med, 2005)

findings: Resisted wrist flexion/pronation may secondarily stress the medial elbow
Passive elbow valgus stress (medial gap) is the definitive joint-play test — a ligament test, not a resisted-muscle one
sttt.interpretation: Resisted wrist flexion/pronation can secondarily stress the medial elbow, but the definitive test is the passive elbow valgus stress test (medial gap) — a ligament/joint-play test rather than a resisted-muscle test.

muscles.name: Wrist Flexors / Pronator Teres (medial flexor-pronator mass)
muscles.state: Protectively overactive supporting a lax UCL

cpa.pattern: The medial flexor-pronator mass may become protectively overactive supporting a lax UCL — check once the acute phase allows. Fascial component (from source): Medial capsuloligamentous fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Medial Elbow / Valgus Screen
functionalScreen.note: Includes both the standard valgus stress test and the Moving Valgus Stress Test (MVST) — the direct named match for this condition.

E07.name: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome (Ulnar Neuropathy at the Elbow)

Intrinsic wasting.text: Wasting of the ulnar-innervated intrinsic hand muscles (first dorsal interosseous, hypothenar) reflects motor axon loss from chronic ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel, indicating a more advanced or severe entrapment.

4th/5th tingling.text: Paresthesia confined to the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger maps precisely to the ulnar nerve's sensory distribution, differentiating this from median (carpal tunnel) or radial nerve entrapments.

Tinel medial.text: A positive Tinel's sign over the cubital tunnel, posterior to the medial epicondyle, indicates mechanosensitivity of irritated axons at the site where the ulnar nerve is compressed beneath the arcuate (Osborne's) ligament.

Sustained elbow-flexion posture.text: Elbow flexion increases cubital tunnel pressure several-fold by tensioning the arcuate ligament over the nerve and narrowing the tunnel; sustained or repetitive flexion (phone use, sleeping with the elbow bent) is the classic aggravating posture in cubital tunnel syndrome.
Sustained elbow-flexion posture.source: Apfelberg & Larson, cubital tunnel pressure studies; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.6

resisted.label: Resisted Ulnar-Innervated Muscles (FCU, ring/little finger FDP)

findings: Resisted ulnar-innervated muscles (FCU, ring/little FDP) may show a weak & painless (neural, not contractile) pattern in advanced cases
Tinel's sign at the elbow, combined with elbow flexion and ULTT-ulnar, is the primary provocation
sttt.interpretation: A weak-and-painless pattern in ulnar-innervated muscles reflects a neural rather than contractile lesion in advanced cases; Tinel's sign at the elbow combined with sustained elbow flexion and the ulnar ULTT is the primary provocation.

cpa.pattern: Grip/Hand Intrinsics inhibited from a neurological (ulnar) cause — differentiate from a simple overuse-inhibition pattern. Fascial component (from source): Ulnar neural tension line.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: ULNT2 (ulnar bias)

fields.label: Cubital tunnel Tinel's (medial) + resisted elbow flexion reproduces symptoms

functionalScreen.note: This setup explicitly includes "cubital tunnel Tinel's (medial) and resisted elbow flexion" — the direct named match.

Tenderness ~4cm distal to lateral epicon.text: Tenderness centered over the arcade of Fröhse (the proximal fibrous edge of supinator), roughly 4cm distal to the lateral epicondyle rather than directly over it, localizes the lesion to radial nerve entrapment rather than the ECRB origin of lateral epicondylalgia — the single most important differentiator between the two conditions.

Repetitive-pronation loading.text: Repetitive forearm pronation/supination increases dynamic compression of the radial nerve as it passes through the radial tunnel and beneath the arcade of Fröhse, provoking or perpetuating radial tunnel syndrome.

findings: Resisted supination and resisted wrist extension both reproduce forearm pain, mimicking lateral epicondylalgia
Pain site is ~4cm distal to the epicondyle, not AT the epicondyle — the key differentiator
sttt.interpretation: Resisted supination and resisted wrist extension both reproduce forearm pain and can mimic lateral epicondylalgia; the key differentiator is that the pain site is roughly 4cm distal to the lateral epicondyle rather than directly over it.

muscles.name: Wrist Extensors
muscles.state: Screen the same group as lateral epicondylalgia — confirm radial-nerve distribution first

cpa.pattern: Screen the same wrist extensor group as lateral epicondylalgia, but confirm the radial-nerve distribution before treating this as a simple tendinopathy. Fascial component (from source): Radial (PIN) neural tension.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: ULNT2b (radial bias)
functionalScreen.note: This app's ULNT2 test explicitly distinguishes a median bias (2a) from a radial bias (2b), matching this specific nerve.

Proximal-volar-forearm tenderness.text: Tenderness over the proximal volar forearm, at the two heads of pronator teres, localizes the compression site of the median nerve as it passes between the muscle's humeral and ulnar heads — proximal to the carpal tunnel and thus a key differentiator from carpal tunnel syndrome.

median signs.text: Sensory or motor changes in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger) confirm median nerve involvement, but with a proximal-forearm provocation pattern rather than the wrist-level provocation typical of carpal tunnel syndrome.

Repetitive-gripping/pronation posture.text: Repetitive resisted gripping combined with forearm pronation increases pronator teres muscle bulk and contraction tension around the median nerve, provoking the dynamic compression characteristic of pronator teres syndrome.

findings: Resisted pronation reproduces forearm pain and may reproduce median-nerve tingling — distinguishes from a simple pronator strain
Resisted wrist flexion may also implicate FCR
Median ULTT may reproduce median symptoms
sttt.interpretation: Resisted pronation reproducing both forearm pain and median-nerve tingling distinguishes pronator teres syndrome from a simple pronator strain; resisted wrist flexion may also implicate the FCR.

cpa.pattern: Pronator Teres overactivity compresses the median nerve — check Biceps/Supinator facilitation as the antagonist pairing. Fascial component (from source): Median neural tension through pronator.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Elbow AROM (pronation/supination) + ULNT2a (median bias)
functionalScreen.note: Cross-references the proximal median entrapment against distal carpal tunnel syndrome by symptom location.

Thenar wasting.text: Atrophy of the median-innervated thenar muscles (particularly abductor pollicis brevis) reflects motor axon loss from chronic median nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum — a late/severe sign, since sensory symptoms typically precede detectable motor wasting.

positive flick sign.text: Symptom relief on shaking the hand (the flick sign) is a historically-cited clinical clue for carpal tunnel syndrome reflecting transient improvement in nerve perfusion/venous return at the wrist, though contemporary diagnostic-accuracy studies show only modest sensitivity, so it should be interpreted alongside Phalen's and Tinel's rather than in isolation.
positive flick sign.source: Pryse-Phillips, Validation of a diagnostic sign in carpal tunnel syndrome, 1984

Sustained wrist-flexion/workstation post.text: Sustained wrist flexion (or extension) raises intracarpal canal pressure, directly compressing the median nerve against the flexor retinaculum — the same postural mechanism exploited provocatively by Phalen's test and the classic ergonomic aggravating factor in CTS.

findings: Resisted finger flexion (FDS/FDP) usually preserved early, weak later as thenar/median intrinsics become affected
Phalen's and Tinel's are passive/positional provocations, not resisted-muscle tests
sttt.interpretation: Resisted finger flexion is usually preserved early and only becomes weak later as the thenar/median intrinsics are affected; Phalen's and Tinel's signs are passive/positional provocations rather than resisted-muscle tests.

cpa.pattern: Grip/Hand Intrinsics inhibited from a neurological (median: thumb/index) cause — differentiate from Pronator Teres syndrome by symptom location and provocation. Fascial component (from source): Flexor retinaculum / median neural line.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Carpal Tunnel Screen (Phalen's / Tinel's / compression test)
functionalScreen.note: The exact, direct named match for this condition. FMA source note: Phalen/Tinel & median ULTT reproduce; grip endurance reduced.

Radial-styloid swelling/tenderness.text: Swelling and tenderness directly over the radial styloid localizes the pathology to the first dorsal compartment, where the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) tendons become thickened and entrapped within their shared fibro-osseous sheath.
Radial-styloid swelling/tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; PMC10437001, First Extensor Wrist Compartment anatomy review

Thumb-loading / new-parent lifting postu.text: Repetitive thumb abduction/extension combined with ulnar deviation — the classic mechanism of lifting an infant under the arms — repeatedly loads the APL/EPB tendons through the fibro-osseous first dorsal compartment, the well-documented mechanism behind postpartum De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

1st dorsal compartment.text: Direct palpation over the first dorsal compartment (APL/EPB tendons at the radial styloid) reproduces localized tenderness that confirms the compartment, rather than the wrist joint or scaphoid, as the pain source.

findings: Resisted thumb extension (EPL/EPB) strong but painful at the 1st dorsal compartment
Resisted thumb abduction (APL) strong but painful at the 1st dorsal compartment
Finkelstein's test is a passive-stretch analogue of the same compartment
sttt.interpretation: Both resisted thumb extension (EPL/EPB) and resisted thumb abduction (APL) are strong but painful over the 1st dorsal compartment; Finkelstein's test is a passive-stretch analogue that reproduces the same compartment pain.

cpa.reason: Not primarily a compensation pattern (tenosynovitis, often repetitive-strain/postpartum) — Wrist Extensor facilitation supports recovery but isn't the root driver. Fascial component (from source): 1st dorsal-compartment fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.reason: No dedicated named test exists in this app's Wrist FMA set — Finkelstein's test (above) is the primary tool; Wrist AROM+Grip serves only as a general baseline.

W03.name: TFCC Tear (Ulnar-Sided Wrist Pain)
keyExams: TFCC stress test (ulnar compression through lunate)

Ulnar-sided swelling.text: Swelling localized to the ulnar aspect of the wrist, between the ulnar styloid and the carpus, reflects synovitis or effusion of the distal radioulnar joint or ulnocarpal space where the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) resides.

clicking.text: An audible or palpable click with wrist rotation or ulnar deviation reflects mechanical catching of a torn or unstable TFCC fragment (or associated DRUJ instability) between the ulnar head and carpus during loaded motion.

Ulnar-loading grip posture.text: Activities that combine grip with ulnar deviation and forearm rotation (e.g. using a screwdriver or racquet sports) axially load the ulnocarpal joint and compress the TFCC between the ulnar head and carpus, the classic aggravating mechanism for TFCC tears.

Ulnar-sided wrist.text: Focal tenderness in the ulnar fovea, between the ulnar styloid and the FCU tendon, is a sensitive localizing sign for TFCC and ulnar-sided pathology and forms the basis of the ulnar fovea sign.
Ulnar-sided wrist.source: Tay et al., validation of the ulnar fovea sign; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7

specialTests: TFCC Stress Test (ulnar compression through lunate)

passive.label: TFCC Stress Test (ulnar compression through lunate)

findings: Resisted wrist extension/flexion is not the primary test here
Passive TFCC stress test (ulnar compression through the lunate) is a definitive joint-play test
Passive ulnar-deviation load is a definitive joint-play test
sttt.interpretation: Resisted wrist extension/flexion is not primary for TFCC pathology; the passive TFCC stress test (ulnar compression through the lunate) and passive ulnar-deviation load are the definitive joint-play tests.

cpa.reason: Not a classic compensation pattern (intra-articular ligament/cartilage) — Wrist Flexor/Extensor balance supports the joint but doesn't address the structural tear. Fascial component (from source): Ulnocarpal / TFCC fascia.

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: TFCC / Ulnar Wrist Screen (ulnar fovea sign, DRUJ stability, piano-key test)
functionalScreen.note: The exact, direct named match for this condition.

Dorsal-radial swelling.text: Localized swelling over the dorsal wrist just distal to Lister's tubercle overlies the scapholunate interval, reflecting synovitis or effusion from disruption of the scapholunate ligament complex.

tenderness.text: Point tenderness in this same dorsal scapholunate interval — the recognized 'SL tenderness spot' just distal to Lister's tubercle — is a classic localizing sign of scapholunate ligament injury.
tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; Watson & Ashmead, scaphoid shift test

FOOSH-guarded posture.text: A fall onto an outstretched, extended, radially-deviated wrist is the classic mechanism disrupting the scapholunate ligament (producing a dorsal intercalated segment instability pattern), and guarding after such an injury reflects protective splinting of the destabilized joint.

findings: Resisted wrist extension is usually painless
Passive Watson scaphoid-shift test (joint-play) is the definitive provocation, not a resisted-muscle test
sttt.interpretation: Resisted wrist extension is usually painless in scapholunate instability; the passive Watson scaphoid-shift test — a joint-play test, not a resisted-muscle test — is the definitive provocation.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (ligamentous instability, typically FOOSH-related).

kineticChain.reason: Not applicable — not modelled in this app's Kinetic Chain library

functionalScreen.name: Scaphoid / Carpal Screen (Watson scaphoid-shift test)
functionalScreen.note: The exact, direct named match for this condition.

W05.name: Wrist Osteoarthritis (Radiocarpal)
keyExams: Imaging referral if not already available

Dorsal swelling.text: Dorsal wrist swelling in radiocarpal OA reflects synovial reaction and capsular distension secondary to degenerative joint change, most prominent dorsally where the capsule is thinnest.

reduced motion.text: Global reduction in wrist flexion/extension reflects a capsular-pattern restriction from cartilage loss, osteophyte formation, and capsular fibrosis, consistent with degenerative joint disease rather than a focal soft-tissue lesion.

crepitus.text: Palpable crepitus during wrist motion reflects roughened articular cartilage and osteophyte formation grinding across the radiocarpal joint surfaces, a hallmark degenerative sign.

Stiff guarded posture.text: A generally stiff, protected resting wrist posture reflects long-standing capsular fibrosis and pain-avoidance behaviour typical of chronic degenerative joint disease rather than an acute soft-tissue injury.

findings: Resisted tests generally painless — non-contractile pattern
Passive wrist flexion/extension both restricted (capsular pattern) with a hard/bony end-feel
Radiocarpal joint-play glide reduced
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing rules out a contractile source; a capsular-pattern restriction with a hard/bony end-feel and reduced radiocarpal joint-play glide is consistent with radiocarpal osteoarthritis.

cpa.pattern: Wrist Extensor/Flexor facilitation supports remaining function around the restricted joint — not a primary driver (joint OA). Fascial component (from source): Radiocarpal capsular fascia.

functionalScreen.note: The direct match for a capsular-pattern/functional-capacity assessment.

W06.name: Distal Radius Fracture (Suspected, Colles/Barton)
keyExams: Urgent imaging referral before further loading

Dinner-fork deformity.text: The classic 'dinner-fork' silhouette reflects dorsal displacement and angulation of the distal radial fragment (the Colles' fracture pattern); visible bony deformity of this kind is itself pathognomonic for fracture and mandates immediate splinting and urgent imaging rather than further manual testing.
Dinner-fork deformity.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; Colles' fracture classification

marked swelling.text: Rapid, marked swelling reflects acute haematoma formation and soft-tissue injury accompanying the fracture, and — combined with deformity — is sufficient on its own to warrant urgent imaging referral before any loading or special testing is attempted.

N/A — immobilise.text: No positional or postural assessment is performed acutely: the priority is immediate splinting/immobilisation of the suspected fracture and urgent imaging referral, since attempting positional loading risks further displacing the fracture fragments and worsening soft-tissue or neurovascular injury.
N/A — immobilise.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; general acute-fracture management principles

sttt.naText: Do NOT resisted-test an acute suspected fracture — deformity/swelling observation and urgent imaging take priority.

W07.name: Scaphoid Fracture (Suspected)
keyExams: Imaging referral (repeat if initial films negative)

Snuffbox swelling/tenderness.text: Swelling and point tenderness within the anatomical snuffbox overlie the scaphoid waist, the most common fracture site and the region with the most precarious blood supply (retrograde flow from distal to proximal), making this finding a critical trigger for imaging even when initial films are negative.
Snuffbox swelling/tenderness.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; scaphoid fracture avascular-necrosis literature

FOOSH.text: A fall onto an outstretched hand is the classic mechanism of scaphoid fracture, with axial compressive/hyperextension load transmitted through the wrist concentrating stress at the scaphoid waist.

N/A — immobilise.text: No postural assessment is performed acutely given the scaphoid's precarious blood supply and the high false-negative rate of initial imaging; immediate thumb-spica immobilisation and referral for repeat or advanced imaging take priority over any positional loading.

Anatomical snuffbox.text: Point tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is the most sensitive clinical sign for scaphoid fracture, reflecting direct palpation over the scaphoid waist through the space bordered by the APL/EPB and EPL tendons.

sttt.naText: Do NOT resisted-test — anatomical snuffbox tenderness and axial thumb-load compression are the passive/positional screens; urgent imaging takes priority given the scaphoid's false-negative rate.

functionalScreen.name: Scaphoid / Carpal Screen (anatomical snuffbox, scaphoid compression)
functionalScreen.note: Appropriate even acutely as a screening tool, but confirmed imaging still takes priority given the scaphoid's false-negative rate.

outcomeMeasures: N/A — acute/medical; functional outcome once appropriate

Squared thumb base.text: The 'squared' appearance of the thumb base reflects dorsoradial subluxation of the first metacarpal on the trapezium with osteophyte formation — a classic deformity of advanced first CMC osteoarthritis.
Squared thumb base.source: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7; Eaton-Littler CMC OA staging

tenderness.text: Point tenderness directly over the first CMC joint line localizes degenerative change to the trapeziometacarpal joint, distinguishing it from more distal thumb pathology such as De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

± crepitus.text: Palpable crepitus with thumb circumduction reflects roughened articular surfaces grinding within the degenerated trapeziometacarpal joint.

Thumb-loading pinch posture.text: Repetitive pinch/grip loading generates high joint reaction forces across the small-surface-area first CMC joint, accelerating cartilage wear and provoking pain — the biomechanical basis for the Grind Test's axial-load provocation.

1st CMC joint.text: Direct palpation over the trapeziometacarpal joint line reproduces localized pain that confirms the joint itself, rather than surrounding soft tissue, as the pain generator.

passive.label: Grind Test (axial load + rotation at 1st CMC)

findings: Resisted thumb tests may be painful, but capsular restriction is more the story
The passive Grind Test (axial load + rotation at the 1st CMC) is the definitive provocation
sttt.interpretation: Resisted thumb tests may be painful, but capsular restriction is the more prominent finding; the passive Grind Test (axial load plus rotation at the 1st CMC) is the definitive provocation.

cpa.reason: Not primarily compensation-driven (joint OA); thumb intrinsic (Grip/Hand Intrinsics) facilitation supports function. Fascial component (from source): 1st CMC capsular fascia.

W09.name: ECU Tendinopathy / Instability
keyExams: Resisted wrist extension in ulnar deviation

Ulnar-dorsal tenderness ± subluxation.text: Tenderness along the ulnar-dorsal wrist over the sixth dorsal compartment localizes pathology to the ECU tendon; a palpable or visible snap/subluxation with forearm rotation indicates instability of the tendon within (or out of) its fibro-osseous subsheath, distinguishing frank instability from simple tendinopathy.

Ulnar-loading forearm posture.text: Combined wrist ulnar deviation with forearm supination increases tension and subluxation risk on the ECU tendon within its sixth-compartment groove — the mechanism reproduced by the ECU synergy test.

ECU tendon.text: Direct palpation of the ECU tendon during resisted ulnar deviation/extension reproduces pain or a palpable snap, confirming the tendon — rather than the TFCC or DRUJ — as the ulnar-sided pain source.

resisted.label: Resisted Wrist Extension in Ulnar Deviation

findings: Resisted wrist extension in ULNAR deviation specifically reproduces the pain — differentiates from ECRB/lateral-epicondylalgia's neutral/radial-deviation resisted extension
ECU synergy test is the functional analogue
sttt.interpretation: Resisted wrist extension specifically in ulnar deviation reproduces the pain, differentiating ECU tendinopathy from lateral epicondylalgia's neutral-or-radial-deviation resisted extension; the ECU synergy test is the functional analogue.

muscles.state: Same group as lateral epicondylalgia — confirm ulnar-sided, extensor-specific pattern

cpa.pattern: Same muscle group as lateral epicondylalgia, but confirm the ulnar-sided, extensor tendinopathy-specific pattern before treating as generic extensor tendinopathy. Fascial component (from source): ECU sheath fascia.

W10.name: Trigger Finger / Flexor Tenosynovitis (Wrist model)
keyExams: Palpation for flexor tendon nodule/catching at A1 pulley
palpation: Flexor tendon nodule/catching at A1 pulley

Palpable A1-pulley nodule.text: A palpable nodule at the A1 pulley, over the metacarpal head, reflects fibrotic thickening or fusiform swelling of the flexor tendon that outgrows the pulley's fixed diameter, initiating the mechanical catching characteristic of stenosing tenosynovitis.

catching.text: Catching or locking of the digit during active flexion-extension reflects the swollen tendon nodule abruptly forcing its way through the narrowed A1 pulley, producing the characteristic 'trigger' snap.

Gripping-load posture.text: Repetitive or sustained gripping increases mechanical friction and load on the flexor tendon as it passes through the A1 pulley, promoting the nodular thickening and tenosynovitis that underlie trigger finger.

Flexor tendon nodule/catching at A1 pull.text: Palpating the flexor tendon directly over the A1 pulley while the patient actively flexes and extends the finger reproduces the catching sensation and confirms the nodule's location at the pulley — the diagnostic reference standard for trigger finger.

passive.label: Palpation at A1 Pulley During Active Flexion-Extension

findings: Resisted finger flexion (FDS/FDP) may reproduce catching, not weakness
Palpation for the A1-pulley nodule during active flexion-extension is the primary provocation
sttt.interpretation: Resisted finger flexion may reproduce catching rather than true weakness; palpation for the A1-pulley nodule during active finger flexion-extension is the primary provocation for trigger finger.

cpa.reason: Not a classic compensation pattern (tendon stenosis, often repetitive-grip driven) — Grip/Hand Intrinsics facilitation is supportive, not corrective. Fascial component (from source): Flexor tendon-sheath (A1 pulley) fascia.

H01.name: Digital Osteoarthritis (Heberden's / Bouchard's Nodes)
keyExams: Inspection/palpation of DIP (Heberden's) and PIP (Bouchard's) nodes

DIP/PIP nodes.text: Firm, bony nodules at the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) reflect osteophyte formation at the joint margins — the classic peripheral joint distribution of primary generalized osteoarthritis in the hand.

deformity.text: Angular deviation at the DIP or PIP joints reflects asymmetric cartilage loss and collateral ligament laxity as the degenerative process progresses, a marker of more advanced joint destruction.

reduced grip.text: Diminished grip strength reflects both pain-inhibited muscle activation and mechanical disadvantage from joint deformity and stiffness across multiple digital joints, a functional consequence of widespread digital OA.

Deforming digit posture.text: A sustained angular or flexed digit posture reflects the joint's adaptation to asymmetric cartilage loss and capsuloligamentous laxity, a structural consequence of chronic osteoarthritic change rather than acute guarding.

DIP (Heberden's) nodes.text: Palpable bony nodules at the DIP joint margins confirm osteophyte formation as the swelling's structural cause, distinguishing this bony end-feel from the soft, fluctuant swelling of synovitis.

PIP (Bouchard's) nodes.text: Palpable bony nodules at the PIP joint margins similarly confirm osteophytic, rather than synovial, swelling at this joint, completing the classic Heberden's/Bouchard's node pattern of hand OA.

findings: Resisted finger flexion/extension generally painless — non-contractile pattern
Passive DIP/PIP motion restricted with a bony end-feel, nodules palpable
sttt.interpretation: Painless resisted testing rules out a contractile source; passive DIP/PIP motion restricted with a bony end-feel and palpable nodules is consistent with digital osteoarthritis.

muscles.name: Grip / Hand Intrinsics
muscles.state: Facilitation supports function around restricted joints

cpa.pattern: Grip/Hand Intrinsics facilitation supports function around the restricted joints — not a primary driver (joint OA). Fascial component (from source): Peri-articular digital fascia.

H02.name: Thumb Ulnar Collateral Ligament Injury (Skier's / Gamekeeper's Thumb)
keyExams: Valgus stress test of the thumb MCP (flexion & extension)
Palpation of ulnar aspect of thumb MCP
Imaging to exclude avulsion fracture (Stener lesion)

Ulnar-MCP swelling/tenderness.text: Swelling and tenderness on the ulnar aspect of the thumb MCP joint localize injury to the ulnar collateral ligament, the primary restraint against valgus (radially-directed) stress at this joint, injured by forced thumb abduction such as a fall onto a ski pole or repetitive gamekeeper-style stress.
Ulnar-MCP swelling/tenderness.source: Wheeless' Textbook of Orthopaedics, Gamekeeper's Thumb; Campbell, 1955

Guarded thumb posture.text: Protective splinting of the thumb in adduction minimizes further valgus stress on the injured or lax UCL, and should prompt caution against aggressive stress testing until a Stener lesion — interposition of the adductor aponeurosis preventing the torn ligament from re-approximating its insertion — has been excluded on imaging.

Ulnar aspect of thumb MCP.text: Focal tenderness over the ulnar aspect of the thumb MCP, near the ligament's insertion at the base of the proximal phalanx, localizes the injury site and — combined with a palpable mass — can be a clinical clue to a Stener lesion, where the ruptured ligament end is trapped superficial to the adductor aponeurosis and cannot heal without surgical repair.
Ulnar aspect of thumb MCP.source: Stener, 1962; Radsource, Ulnar Collateral Ligament Tears of the Thumb

specialTests: Valgus Stress Test — Thumb MCP (flexion & extension)

passive.label: Valgus Stress — Thumb MCP in Flexion
Valgus Stress — Thumb MCP in Extension

findings: Passive valgus stress of the thumb MCP (in flexion AND extension) is the definitive joint-play test
sttt.interpretation: Passive valgus stress testing of the thumb MCP in both flexion and extension is the definitive joint-play test — a resisted-muscle test is not the primary tool for this ligamentous injury.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (acute ligament sprain) — imaging to exclude a Stener lesion takes priority. Fascial component (from source): Ulnar MCP capsuloligamentous fascia.

H03.name: Trigger Finger / Thumb (Stenosing Flexor Tenosynovitis, Hand model)
keyExams: Palpation for A1-pulley nodule / catching on active flexion-extension
Observation of triggering / locking of the digit
palpation: A1-pulley nodule / catching on active flexion-extension

A1-pulley nodule.text: As with the wrist-model presentation of this condition, a palpable nodule at the A1 pulley reflects fibrotic thickening of the flexor tendon outgrowing the fixed pulley diameter, the structural basis for triggering.

catching/locking.text: Catching progressing to frank locking of the digit, requiring passive correction, reflects a more advanced stage of stenosing tenosynovitis in which the nodule can no longer reliably pass through the narrowed pulley.

Gripping-load posture.text: As in the wrist-model presentation, repetitive gripping increases friction and load on the flexor tendon at the A1 pulley, promoting the nodular thickening that produces triggering.

A1-pulley nodule / catching on active fl.text: Palpating over the A1 pulley during active finger flexion-extension directly reproduces the catching and confirms the pulley as the mechanical block — the same diagnostic manoeuvre used for the wrist-model presentation of this condition.

passive.label: Palpation at A1 Pulley During Active Flexion-Extension

findings: Palpation for the A1-pulley nodule during active flexion-extension is the primary provocation, not a resisted-strength test — same logic as the wrist-model version of this condition
sttt.interpretation: As with the wrist-model version of this condition, palpation for the A1-pulley nodule during active flexion-extension is the primary provocation rather than a resisted-strength test.

cpa.pattern: Grip/Hand Intrinsics facilitation is supportive only here, not corrective for the underlying tendon stenosis. Fascial component (from source): Flexor tendon-sheath (A1 pulley) fascia.

H04.name: Dupuytren's Contracture (Palmar Fascia)
keyExams: Palpation of palmar fascia cords/nodules (ring/little finger)

Palmar cord/nodule.text: A palpable, firm cord or nodule in the palmar fascia, most often over the ring/little finger rays, reflects pathological fibroblastic proliferation and collagen deposition within the palmar aponeurosis — the pathoanatomic hallmark of Dupuytren's disease.
Palmar cord/nodule.source: Orthobullets, Dupuytren's Disease; StatPearls, Dupuytren Contracture

ring/little-finger flexion contracture.text: Fixed flexion deformity at the MCP and/or PIP joints of the ring and little fingers reflects progressive shortening of the diseased longitudinal palmar cords, which selectively involve the ulnar rays far more often than the radial digits.
ring/little-finger flexion contracture.source: Orthobullets, Dupuytren's Disease; StatPearls, Dupuytren Contracture

Fixed digit-flexion posture.text: A digit held in fixed flexion reflects mechanical shortening by the mature Dupuytren cord rather than active muscular guarding — the deformity does not passively correct because the pathology is a structural fascial contracture, not a soft-tissue or joint-capsule tightness, which is precisely what the Hueston tabletop test exposes.
Fixed digit-flexion posture.source: Hueston, The Table Top Test, 1982; StatPearls, Dupuytren Contracture

Palmar fascia cords/nodules (ring/little.text: Direct palpation of firm, longitudinally-oriented cords within the palmar fascia, typically along the ring/little finger rays, confirms the fascial (not tendinous) origin of the contracture — the cords are adherent to the skin and do not glide independently of it.

findings: Not a resisted-muscle test — the palmar fascia is non-contractile
Hueston tabletop test (passive/positional) is a definitive test
MCP/PIP passive extension deficit measurement is a definitive test
sttt.interpretation: Dupuytren's contracture is not tested with resisted-muscle tests since the palmar fascia is non-contractile; the Hueston tabletop test and MCP/PIP passive extension deficit measurement are the definitive tests.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (fascial disease process).

functionalScreen.note: The composite-fist and extension components directly quantify the flexion contracture.

H05.name: Finger Sprain / Collateral Ligament Injury (Jammed Finger)
keyExams: Collateral ligament stress test of the affected joint

Fusiform joint swelling.text: Spindle-shaped ('fusiform') swelling localized to a single interphalangeal joint reflects capsular/collateral ligament injury and intra-articular effusion at that joint following an axial or angular stress — a pattern distinct from the diffuse digit swelling seen in infection or the multi-joint pattern of inflammatory arthritis.

jammed history.text: A reported 'jammed finger' mechanism — an axial load to the fingertip, often from catching a ball — is the classic history for collateral ligament sprain or volar plate injury at the PIP/DIP joint, and should always prompt screening for a concurrent avulsion fracture.

Guarded digit posture.text: Holding the injured digit in slight flexion and protecting it from contact minimizes tension on the injured collateral ligament/capsule, a typical protective posture following an acute sprain.

findings: Passive collateral ligament stress test (affected joint) is the definitive joint-play test
Active DIP/PIP extension screens for a concurrent extensor-tendon injury (mallet/boutonniere) rather than testing a specific muscle
sttt.interpretation: The passive collateral ligament stress test of the affected joint is the definitive joint-play test; active DIP/PIP extension screens for a concurrent extensor-tendon injury (mallet or boutonniere) rather than testing a specific muscle.

cpa.reason: Not a compensation-pattern condition (acute ligament sprain).

H06.name: Raynaud's Phenomenon (Vascular Differential)
keyExams: History of triphasic colour change (white-blue-red) with cold
Screen for secondary causes (connective tissue disease) if atypical

Triphasic colour change (white-blue-red).text: The sequential white (vasospasm/ischaemia), blue (cyanosis from static deoxygenated blood), then red (reactive hyperaemic flushing on rewarming) colour change reflects the classic vasospasm-then-reperfusion sequence of digital arterioles in response to cold or emotional stress; this triphasic pattern is the defining diagnostic feature distinguishing Raynaud's phenomenon from other causes of cold hands.
Triphasic colour change (white-blue-red).source: LeRoy & Medsger, Raynaud's phenomenon classification criteria; Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment, Ch.7

N/A.text: Posture is not assessed because Raynaud's phenomenon is a vasospastic vascular reflex, not a musculoskeletal or biomechanical condition — no resting position or loading posture influences vasospasm risk the way it would for a joint, tendon, or nerve entrapment lesion.
N/A.source: LeRoy & Medsger, Raynaud's phenomenon classification criteria
